About Gobaris

Rooted in Braj.
Returned to the soil.

Gobaris began with a simple observation: Braj has always fed its cows before it fed anything else — and what they leave behind was too valuable to waste. This is the story of how we turn that into compost, the old way.

Read our story Get in touch
Why we started

A land that has always given back.

Some richness isn't worn. Some of it is returned to the soil.

Braj is cow country before it is anything else — temples, lanes, and fields that have shared space with cattle for centuries. For just as long, what those cows leave behind has quietly gone to waste: burned, dumped, or left to dry in the sun instead of going back into the ground it came from.

Gobaris exists to close that loop. We work with gaushalas and farmers across the Braj region to collect cow dung and turn it into vermicompost the traditional way — no shortcuts, no synthetic accelerants, just moisture, microbes, and earthworms doing what they've always done.

It isn't fast. A batch takes weeks to become the dark, crumbly compost that leaves our facility. But we'd rather ship something the soil actually recognizes than something that just looks like fertilizer on a shelf.

The problem

Soil doesn't recover on its own timeline anymore.

Decades of chemical fertilizer use have left a lot of Indian farmland running on borrowed fertility — quick yields today, thinner soil every season after. Even in Braj, where cow dung has always been abundant, most of it never makes it back into the ground in a form plants can use.

Meanwhile, farmers and home gardeners looking for a genuine organic alternative are often stuck choosing between compost that's rushed, poorly sourced, or cut with fillers to bulk it up — and the real thing, which is harder to find and harder to trust without seeing where it came from.

We think that gap is worth closing properly, not quickly.

How we make it

Nature never rushes — so neither do we.

Every batch follows the same five steps. Skip one, and the compost either burns hot and kills the microbial life, or never fully stabilizes at all.

01

Optimal moisture

Moisture activates microbes and speeds decomposition — kept like a wrung-out sponge, damp but never soggy.

02

Balanced carbon & nitrogen

Dry matter for structure, fresh gobar for nutrients — a careful ratio keeps the pile breaking down without overheating or rotting.

03

Worm inoculation

Earthworms are introduced once the pile has softened, converting partly decomposed matter into nutrient-rich castings.

04

Time & curing

Heat reduces, harmful gases escape, and microbial life multiplies. Curing is what makes the compost safe and stable.

05

Ready for your soil

Dark, crumbly, and earthy-smelling — sieved fine, tested, and packed by weight before it leaves us.

Composting 101

5 Signs Your Vermicompost Is Ready to Use

6 MIN READ

It's tempting to treat compost like bread in an oven — set a timer, walk away, come back when it's "done." But vermicompost doesn't work on a clock. It works on conditions, and the only real way to know it's ready is to look, feel, and smell it for yourself. Here's what to check for.

1. It looks like dark, crumbly soil — not scraps

Finished vermicompost should be uniformly dark brown to black, with a loose, crumbly texture similar to coffee grounds. If you can still make out recognizable pieces of vegetable peel, cardboard, or eggshell, it needs more time. Those materials should have broken down into something that no longer resembles what you put in.

2. It smells like a forest floor, not garbage

This is the fastest test. Ready compost has a clean, earthy smell — the kind you get after rain. If it smells sour, ammonia-like, or like rotting food, something's off: usually too much moisture, not enough air, or it simply hasn't cured long enough.

3. The worms have started to move away from it

In an active worm bin, the worms concentrate wherever the freshest food is. As a section finishes composting, you'll notice fewer worms in it — they migrate toward newer material. A finished patch that's mostly worm-free is often a good sign it's ready to harvest.

4. It's stopped heating up

During active decomposition, a compost pile can get noticeably warm as microbes work through the material. Once that activity slows and the pile settles to roughly room temperature, the intense breakdown phase is over and curing is either complete or nearly there.

5. It holds moisture without turning to mush

Finished compost should feel like a well wrung-out sponge — damp, but not dripping, and not falling apart into slurry when you squeeze a handful. If it's soggy and compacted, give it more time and a bit more airflow before using it.

If your compost checks most of these boxes, it's ready to work into soil, mix into potting mix, or use as a top dressing. If it's not quite there, that's normal — the difference between "almost" and "ready" is usually just another week or two of patience.

Guides

How Much Compost Does Your Garden Actually Need?

7 MIN READ

One of the most common questions we hear isn't "does compost work" — it's "how much do I actually use?" Too little and you won't notice a difference; too much, and you're wasting a good resource. Here's a rough, practical guide to get you in the right range. Treat these as starting points, not exact prescriptions — soil, climate, and plant type all shift the numbers a little.

Potted plants

For an established potted plant, mixing in roughly a quarter to half a kilogram of vermicompost per season is a reasonable amount for a medium-sized pot, worked gently into the top few centimetres of soil without disturbing the roots too much. For a new potting mix, compost can make up about a quarter to a third of the total volume, blended with regular potting soil.

Raised beds and vegetable patches

A commonly used rule of thumb is a layer of compost roughly 2 to 5 centimetres deep, worked into the top 15–20 centimetres of soil before planting. For beds you replant every season, a lighter top-up layer before each new cycle is usually enough to keep the soil in good shape.

New or tired ground

If you're reviving soil that's been farmed hard or hasn't been amended in years, a heavier initial application — closer to 5 centimetres worked in deeply — gives the soil biology more to work with. After that first season, you can usually taper down to lighter maintenance doses.

Lawns

For lawns, a thin top-dressing layer, roughly half a centimetre spread evenly and worked in with a rake, once or twice a year, is generally enough to improve soil structure without smothering the grass.

Whatever you're growing, it's almost always safer to under-apply and top up later than to overdo it in one go. Vermicompost is gentle enough that it's hard to "burn" plants the way synthetic fertilizer can — but more isn't automatically better. Start modest, watch how your plants respond over a season, and adjust from there.

Soil Health

Why Chemical Fertilizer Tires Soil Out

6 MIN READ

Chemical fertilizer isn't a myth — it does make plants grow, often quickly and visibly. That's exactly why it's so widely used. But there's a difference between feeding a plant and feeding the soil it grows in, and over time, that difference adds up to soil that needs more and more help just to perform the same as before.

It feeds the plant, not the ecosystem beneath it

Synthetic fertilizers deliver nutrients in a form plants can absorb almost immediately — which sounds efficient, but it skips the microbial community that would normally break down organic matter and cycle nutrients naturally. Without regular organic input, that underground ecosystem of bacteria, fungi, and other organisms has less and less to live on, and soil structure and fertility become increasingly dependent on the next bag of fertilizer.

Salts build up over repeated use

Many synthetic fertilizers are salt-based compounds. Used repeatedly without enough organic matter to buffer them, they can gradually raise soil salinity, which makes it harder for plant roots to take up water and can damage the very microbial life that keeps soil healthy in the long run.

Nutrients wash away instead of staying put

Because synthetic fertilizers release nutrients quickly, a good portion can leach away with rain or irrigation before plants ever use it — which is part of why it needs reapplying so often. Organic matter, by contrast, acts like a sponge, holding onto nutrients and moisture and releasing them gradually as plants need them.

What organic amendments do differently

Compost and vermicompost work on a slower, steadier timeline. Instead of directly force-feeding the plant, they feed the soil biology, which in turn makes nutrients available to roots over weeks rather than days. It's a less dramatic effect in the short term, but it builds soil that keeps improving instead of soil that keeps needing more input just to stay the same.

None of this means chemical fertilizer has no place — for some situations it's a genuinely useful tool. But if the goal is soil that gets healthier every season instead of just surviving it, organic matter has to be part of the plan, not an occasional afterthought.

Guides

A Beginner's Guide to Composting at Home

8 MIN READ

Composting looks intimidating from the outside — ratios, temperatures, worm species — but the actual practice comes down to a handful of things done reasonably well. Here's what actually matters when you're just starting out.

Balance your greens and browns

"Greens" are nitrogen-rich materials — vegetable scraps, fruit peels, coffee grounds, fresh grass clippings. "Browns" are carbon-rich — dry leaves, cardboard, shredded paper, straw. A healthy pile needs both: too many greens and it turns slimy and smelly; too many browns and it breaks down painfully slowly. A rough starting ratio is about two to three parts browns for every one part greens by volume.

Keep it damp, not wet

Moisture is what activates the microbes doing the actual work. The pile should feel like a wrung-out sponge — damp to the touch but not dripping. Too dry and decomposition stalls; too wet and the pile can go anaerobic, which is usually when the bad smells start.

Give it air

Composting is largely an aerobic process — it needs oxygen. Turning the pile every week or two, or simply making sure it isn't packed down too tightly, keeps air moving through it and prevents the anaerobic conditions that slow things down and cause odor.

Know what not to add

Meat, dairy, oily foods, and diseased plant material are best left out of a home compost pile — they attract pests, smell badly as they break down, and diseased plants can reintroduce pathogens back into your garden. Stick to fruit and vegetable scraps, yard trimmings, coffee grounds, eggshells, and plain paper or cardboard.

Be patient with it

Depending on the method, temperature, and how much attention you give it, home composting typically takes anywhere from a couple of months to closer to a year. Vermicomposting, where worms do a lot of the work, tends to be on the faster end of that range when it's fed and maintained consistently.

Composting rewards consistency more than effort. A modest bin that gets fed and turned regularly will usually outperform an elaborate setup that gets ignored for weeks at a time. Start small, pay attention to how it looks and smells, and adjust as you go.

Culture & Roots

The Role Cow Dung Has Played in Braj for Centuries

5 MIN READ

Long before vermicomposting had a name, the Braj region already had a working relationship with what its cows left behind. Cows have held a central place in the culture and daily life of this land for generations, and that relationship was never purely spiritual — it was practical too.

Fuel, plaster, and everyday material

Across rural India, and Braj is no exception, dried cow dung cakes have traditionally been used as fuel for cooking fires, valued for burning slow and steady. Mixed with mud, dung has also long been used to plaster and coat the floors and walls of homes — a natural material that's said to help regulate temperature and even helps repel insects, a practice many households in the region still carry on today.

A return to the fields

Perhaps the most enduring use, though, has been agricultural. Long before synthetic fertilizer existed, farmers in Braj and across India relied on cow dung, often composted with straw and other farm waste, to keep their fields fertile season after season. It wasn't seen as waste to dispose of — it was seen as something the land was owed back.

What's changed, and what hasn't

Modern agriculture shifted many farmers toward chemical fertilizers over the past decades, often for good short-term reasons — faster results, easier logistics. But the underlying idea that dung belongs back in the soil never really left; it just moved to the background for a while. Vermicomposting is, in a lot of ways, a more refined, faster version of what farmers in this region already understood: that earthworms and time can turn dung into something soil actively wants.

That's really the throughline for us — not inventing something new, but paying closer attention to a practice that's been quietly running in the background of this land for a very long time, and doing it a little more deliberately.
